source_review.notes: Checked official Google SRE capacity, overload, failure, and launch guidance; current Apache Flink state, elastic-scaling, and autoscaler documentation; current Apache Spark configuration and monitoring documentation; current Kubernetes resource-management guidance; and current Google Cloud Dataflow planning/autoscaling guidance. All thirteen final references returned HTTP 200. Runtime and provider behavior is attributed.

evidence: Reviewed workload-rate, per-class resource demand, effective resource units, target utilization, batch work/window, streaming output, backlog, recovery duration, state, parallelism, and lead-time notation.
Checked dimensional consistency for workload rate times demand, resource units, batch work divided by time/utilization, and backlog divided by catch-up duration.
Checked distinctions among rates, stocks, concurrency, elapsed time, physical units, effective units, useful parallelism, and billed allocation.
notation_and_syntax.notes: All bounds require aligned workload, resource, topology, configuration, and time boundaries; demand coefficients are conditional measurements rather than universal constants.

evidence: Executed the Python 3 fixture and reproduced a 384,000-events/s planned peak, 46.08 cores of offered CPU demand, and a 71-effective-core lower bound at 65% target utilization.
Recomputed a ten-minute average-rate outage backlog as 144,000,000 events, the 30-minute excess catch-up rate as 80,000 events/s, and recovery output as 320,000 events/s.
Recomputed two-copy amplified state as 33.38 GiB and effective state memory at a 60% target as 55.63 GiB using the unrounded value.
numerical_recomputation.notes: The fixture presents independent lower bounds; a deployable shape must also satisfy storage, network, state, partition, dependency, placement, failure, and process/system reserves.

evidence: Verified class workload rate times per-unit demand yields offered demand at each resource and division by target utilization yields a lower bound on effective units.
Verified batch completion is bounded by both per-resource work/capacity and the precedence-constrained critical path.
Verified recovery service must exceed continuing input by backlog divided by catch-up duration, yielding output capacity at least input plus Q/R.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The resource-demand model is valid only within its measured envelope; queueing, skew, retries, spill, and overload can change demand nonlinearly.

evidence: Reviewed zero/low/average/peak/burst/launch workloads, seasonality, long-term growth, backfills, schema/retention changes, and demand-mix drift.
Reviewed cold/warm operation, saturation knees, checkpoints, compaction, state migration, recovery, continuing input, retries, quotas, and dependency overload.
Reviewed indivisible keys/partitions, source/sink limits, fragmented placement, node/rack/zone loss, correlated demand/failure, autoscaling delay, and unavailable capacity.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Expected, high, launch, maintenance, and failure scenarios remain separate so headroom is neither omitted nor double counted.

evidence: Traced forecast workload units into benchmark/production demand measurements and correct output rather than attempted or accepted work.
Checked batch boundary through input readiness, startup, scheduling, execution, retries, checkpoints, commit, validation, cleanup, and downstream deadline.
Checked streaming conservation through input, backlog, event-time progress, state, checkpoints, recovery, catch-up, sink durability, loss, expiry, and deduplication.
invariant_checking.notes: A plan is feasible only when every resource, stock, parallelism, placement, dependency, reliability, and objective constraint holds simultaneously.

evidence: Reviewed the multi-class resource-demand bound and its target-utilization interpretation.
Reviewed batch work/capacity and critical-path lower bounds, including why perfect division cannot be assumed.
Reviewed recovery backlog conservation and the necessity of excess service while new traffic continues.
proof_review.notes: Lower bounds and forecasts do not prove attainable schedules; representative load, overload, failure, recovery, and placement experiments remain required.

evidence: Audited demand forecast, service demand, capacity envelope, headroom, deadline capacity, sustainable capacity, catch-up capacity, critical path, parallelism ceiling, reserve, and lead time.
Confirmed requested, allocated, physical, effective, usable, reserved, standby, replica, and billed capacity are not conflated.
Confirmed average, peak, burst, forecast scenario, lower bound, tested envelope, and guaranteed objective are labeled distinctly.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Autoscaling is described as bounded delayed allocation within an engineered envelope, not as capacity creation.

evidence: Reviewed rates/volumes, CPU/memory/state, storage bytes/requests, network/shuffle, keys/partitions, queues/backlog, watermarks, latency, checkpoints, recovery, retries, failures, quotas, and costs.
Reviewed segmentation by workload class, pipeline/tenant, code/data/configuration, operator/stage/partition/key, resource/topology, scenario, time horizon, and forecast version.
Confirmed demand coefficients, forecast ranges, scenario assumptions, actual-versus-plan error, provisioning milestones, and validation runs remain traceable.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: Historical node count, peak short-run throughput, average rate, or low aggregate CPU is not mislabeled as a complete capacity plan.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed objective boundaries, workload forecasts, measured demand, multiple resource centers, batch deadlines, streaming stability, recovery catch-up, state/checkpoints, parallelism, failure reserve, headroom, elasticity, shared governance, nonlinear validation, cost, and feedback.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed implementable scenarios, demand inventories, capacity bounds, topology recomputation, autoscaling limits, quota lead time, load/overload tests, recovery drills, trigger thresholds, owners, and forecast reconciliation. Internal practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified progression from capacity vocabulary and core bounds through batch/stream/state/recovery planning, failure/elasticity constraints, validation, and control loops. Ten examples and five answered exercises cover CPU, backlog, state, batch, parallelism, placement, autoscaling, and evidence.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external Google/Flink/Spark/Kubernetes/Dataflow maintainer, forecasting/statistics/performance/runtime/storage/network/platform/SRE/FinOps/security specialist, production operator, capacity/procurement owner, downstream consumer, affected user, governance or accessibility specialist, or certification review is claimed.
